title: High fidelity control of superconducting qubits with optical transmitted signal
authors: Yu-Huai Li, Daojin Fan, Na Li, Fusheng Chen, Shaowei Li, Dong-Dong Li, Yu Xu, Jin Lin, Ming Gong, He-Liang Huang, Hui Deng, Yulin Wu, Haoran Qian, Shaojun Guo, Futian Liang, Xiaobo Zhu, Cheng-Zhi Peng, Jian-Wei Pan
abstract: Superconducting circuits exhibit remarkable potential for constructing large-scale quantum simulation and computation systems, featuring numerous qubits, extended coherence time, and precise control. Nevertheless, the growing number of signal cables poses a challenge in dilution refrigerators due to space and heat load constraints. To overcome this issue, we experimentally implemented an optically-assisted transmission line as an alternative to coaxial cables. By modulating microwave signals on laser intensities at room temperature and regenerating the signals at a cryogenic plate within the dilution refrigerator, we demonstrated full control of superconducting qubits using photocurrent. We demonstrate and benchmark both single-qubit and two-qubit gates on frequency tunable transmon qubits, achieving fidelities of 99.915% $\pm$ 0.005% and 99.676% $\pm$ 0.041%, respectively, which have reached the requirement of the surface code.
summary: This paper presents an experimental breakthrough for scaling superconducting quantum processors by replacing bulky coaxial cables with an optically-assisted transmission line. By modulating microwave signals onto laser light, the control signals are transmitted to the qubits, significantly reducing heat load in the cryostat. The achieved high-fidelity quantum gates demonstrate a viable path toward building large-scale quantum computers.
main_problem: Scaling superconducting quantum processors is limited by the heat load and space constraints imposed by numerous signal coaxial cables within dilution refrigerators.
main_result: The authors successfully demonstrated full control of superconducting qubits using an optically-assisted transmission line, achieving single-qubit and two-qubit gate fidelities that meet surface code requirements.
method: Microwave control signals are modulated onto laser intensities at room temperature and regenerated at a cryogenic plate using photodiodes, replacing traditional coaxial cables.
model_or_system: The system utilizes frequency tunable transmon superconducting qubits operating at millikelvin temperatures inside a dilution refrigerator. The control mechanism relies on converting microwave signals to optical signals for transmission.
key_observables: Single-qubit gate fidelity (99.915%), two-qubit CZ gate fidelity (99.676%), and measured noise Power Spectral Density (PSD) of the control signal.
important_parameters: Gate fidelities meeting surface code requirements, heat dissipation limits of the cryostat stages (e.g., 4 K stage), and noise spectral density components ($1/f$, white, Lorentzian).
main_assumptions: The most feasible configuration for large-scale systems involves regenerating the control signal at the 4 K stage, and the noise analysis depends on parameters like slope efficiency of the DML.
figures_summary: Figures detail the experimental setups for noise characterization and qubit performance using optical transmission. Tables quantify heat dissipation across different cryostat stages.
paper_structure: The paper progresses from identifying the scaling bottleneck (cables/heat load) to proposing the optical solution, detailing the experimental implementation, characterizing the noise sources (PSD fitting), and finally benchmarking the achieved gate fidelities against theoretical requirements.
why_interesting: This work directly addresses a critical engineering bottleneck in superconducting quantum computing—interconnects—by integrating quantum optics into cryogenic quantum hardware, which is highly relevant for open quantum systems research.

The LD was a directly modulated laser with a center wavelength of 1490 nm.
